**Designing the Control Plane / Data Plane Split and Resilience Invariants**

I will structure the solution around a strict separation between an authoring/governance control plane and a low-latency serving data plane, because the single most important resilience invariant is that flag evaluation must never block or depend on the control plane's availability. The control plane will consist of a Git-based Flag Registry as the canonical source of truth, a Change API/UI that funnels all writes through PRs, an OPA-based policy engine, and CI validation. The data plane will be built from immutable, versioned config snapshots in an object store plus metadata DB, fanned out via pub/sub and regional caches, with optional sidecars/daemons exposing localhost evaluation. I must ensure the SDKs hold both LKG and LKG-1 snapshots — LKG for serving during outages, LKG-1 for corruption protection and instant rollback — and that snapshots are KMS-signed with monotonic version numbers so clients can detect tampering and ordering violations. I will also mandate strict timeouts and circuit breakers on any fetch path so flag delivery can never add tail latency to production traffic. Multi-region active/active distribution with per-region caches handles partition survival; the P0/P1/P2 alert tiers later map directly onto this: control plane UI/API down is only P2 precisely because serving is unaffected.

**Structuring the Flag Model, GitOps Promotion Pipeline, and Environment Overlays**

For multi-environment rollouts I will define a canonical flag model with four types — release, ops/kill-switch, experiment, and permission/entitlement — each carrying mandatory metadata (`owner_team`, `risk_level`, `expires_at/ttl`, `rollback_plan`, `environments_allowed`, ticket links) so governance and TTL automation have structured data to act on. Environments (`dev`, `staging`, `prod-canary`, `prod`) share the same flag key but differ via base definition + environment overlay + optional region overlay; promotion is always a pointer move to an immutable snapshot id, never a mutable edit, which makes diffs deterministic and rollbacks trivial. The pipeline stages must be: PR creation → CI validation (schema checks, safety lint like "no 100% on in prod without approvals," determinism/bucketing checks, PII policy checks, and unit-like evaluation tests asserting targeting outcomes for sample contexts) → governance gate scaled by risk level and environment → snapshot build (minimized, indexed, signed) → progressive promotion → post-deploy verification before auto-ramping. I will also bake in flag-debt prevention: TTL alerts before expiration and optional auto-disable past TTL for release flags, with a retire step (remove code + flag) as the terminal lifecycle state.

**Hardening Rollback Automation, Governance Policy-as-Code, and SDK Compatibility**

Rollback must operate via flag changes, not redeploys, so I will layer four mechanisms: an instant kill-switch flag with highest precedence, pointer reversion to the LKG-1 snapshot id, auto-pause of ramps on guardrail failure, and full auto-rollback driven by error-budget breaches. The rollout controller will execute a 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% ramp with bake times, comparing canary vs baseline on service SLOs (5xx, p95 latency, OOM, db errors), feature metrics (checkout completion, payment auth rate), and client signals (crash-free sessions); threshold breaches for N minutes freeze and page, severe breaches trigger snapshot reversion plus kill-switch. For governance, I will encode segregation of duties in OPA: high-risk prod changes require owner + on-call approver who is not the author + security approval + linked ticket; sensitive-attribute targeting triggers privacy review; billing/entitlement flags require finance sign-off. The audit log must be immutable (optionally WORM/append-only) capturing author, approvers, diff, snapshot id, and reason, with a break-glass role that is time-bound, MFA-gated, and incident-linked. On SDK versioning, I will anchor everything to a stable evaluation contract — adopting OpenFeature as the API with a custom provider — and define a snapshot schema version negotiated against SDK-declared supported versions. Semantic versioning governs SDK releases (PATCH fixes, MINOR compatible operators, MAJOR breaking semantics), with the control plane obligated to emit snapshots compatible with N-2 SDK majors; telemetry carrying `sdk_name`/`sdk_version`/`schema_version` feeds a deprecation dashboard, automated EOL tickets, and blocking of prod changes requiring features absent from deployed SDKs.

**Wiring Telemetry, Correlation, and On-Call Operational Workflows**

Finally, I need three telemetry streams — control-plane change events (who/what/snapshot id/rollout transitions), data-plane evaluation telemetry (counts by flag/variation/reason, eval latency, cache freshness, fetch failures), and privacy-minimized, sampled exposure events for experimentation — plus operational metrics on per-region snapshot distribution lag, fanout success, and error budgets for stale config and evaluation failures. Correlation is the key design choice: snapshot id and flag evaluation context ride along in traces/logs as baggage fields, enabling an automated change-impact view overlaying flag changes on service health charts. For on-call, I will define concrete SLOs (99.9% of instances receive a snapshot within 60s; 99.99% local evaluation success; p99 eval < 1ms) and tiered alerts, then pair them with standard runbooks — rollback last prod snapshot, engage kill-switch, global rollout freeze, validate snapshot signature, region-isolated distribution failure, SDK bug pinning. Change management integration closes the loop: every prod rollout links an incident/change record, auto-creates a Slack/Teams bake-monitoring channel, and change freeze windows are enforced by the same OPA policy engine, so governance, telemetry, and incident response all share the snapshot id as the unifying correlation key.
</think>

## 1) Design goals (resilience + safety)
- **Serving never blocks production traffic**: if the flag control plane is down, applications still evaluate using **last-known-good** config with safe defaults.
- **Fast, controlled change propagation**: seconds to minutes to reach all regions with bounded blast radius.
- **Auditable governance**: who changed what, why, when, and which approval policy allowed it.
- **Multi-environment promotion**: dev → staging → prod with deterministic config diffs and environment overrides.
- **Automated rollback**: rollback via flag changes (not redeploys), triggered manually or by telemetry guardrails.
- **SDK compatibility**: versioned evaluation contract; older SDKs continue to function during platform evolution.
- **Operational excellence**: clear on-call runbooks, alerting, change freezes, and break-glass access.

---

## 2) Reference architecture (control plane vs data plane)
**Control plane (authoring + governance)**
- **Flag Registry (GitOps)**: canonical flag definitions in a repo (YAML/JSON + schema).
- **Change API/UI**: writes go through PRs or an API that auto-generates PRs.
- **Policy/Approval Engine**: “policy-as-code” (e.g., OPA) enforcing approvals, ownership, and risk rules.
- **CI Validation**: schema validation, rule linting, safety checks, diff previews, and test evaluation.

**Data plane (low-latency delivery + evaluation)**
- **Config Snapshot Store**: versioned, immutable snapshots per environment (e.g., object store + metadata DB).
- **Distribution**: fanout via pub/sub + regional caches (or CDN) to minimize latency and survive partitions.
- **Edge/Sidecar/Daemon (optional but common)**: local cache + streaming updates; apps query localhost.
- **SDKs**: evaluate locally from cached snapshots; refresh via streaming/polling; never hard-depend on control plane.

**Resilience patterns**
- Multi-region active/active distribution; per-region config caches.
- Snapshots are **signed** (KMS) and include monotonic version numbers.
- Clients keep **LKG (last known good)** + **LKG-1** for quick rollback and corruption protection.
- Strict timeouts and circuit breakers: flag fetch must not add tail latency.

---

## 3) Flag model + lifecycle (avoid “flag debt”)
**Flag types**
- *Release* (temporary), *Ops/Kill-switch*, *Experiment*, *Permission/Entitlement* (high governance).

**Required metadata**
- `owner_team`, `service_owners`, `jira/change_ticket`, `data_classification`, `risk_level`, `created_at`, `expires_at/ttl`, `rollback_plan`, `dependencies`, `environments_allowed`.

**Lifecycle automation**
- Create → implement (default off) → test in dev → stage → progressive prod rollout → ramp to 100% → **retire** (remove code + flag).
- TTL enforcement: alerts before expiration; optional auto-disable past TTL for release flags.

---

## 4) Multi-environment rollout pipeline (GitOps promotion)
### Environment strategy
- Separate namespaces: `dev`, `staging`, `prod` (and optionally `prod-canary`, `prod-eu`, etc.).
- Same flag key across envs; config differs by **overlay**:
  - Base definition (global) + environment overlay + region overlay (optional).
- Promotion is a **versioned snapshot**: `prod` always points to an immutable snapshot id.

### Pipeline stages
1. **PR creation**
   - Developer adds/edits flag definition.
2. **CI validation**
   - Schema checks; rule safety lint (e.g., no “100% on” in prod without approvals).
   - Determinism check (bucketing stable); forbidden attributes; PII policy checks.
   - “Evaluate tests”: unit-like tests that assert expected targeting outcomes for sample contexts.
3. **Governance gate**
   - Approval policy based on `risk_level` and environment:
     - dev: team approval
     - staging: team + QA
     - prod: team + on-call owner + (security/compliance for high-risk)
4. **Snapshot build**
   - Compile to a normalized snapshot format used by SDKs (minimized, indexed).
   - Sign snapshot and publish to snapshot store.
5. **Progressive rollout orchestration**
   - Promote snapshot to `staging`, then `prod-canary`, then `prod`.
   - Rollout rules include *percentage*, *cohort allowlist*, *region*, *service instance*.
6. **Post-deploy verification**
   - Automated monitors validate health before auto-ramping.

---

## 5) Rollback automation (guardrails + safe switches)
### Rollback mechanisms
- **Instant kill-switch**: an ops flag that disables a feature regardless of other rules (highest precedence).
- **Revert to previous snapshot**: promote `LKG-1` snapshot id back to environment pointer.
- **Auto-pause ramp**: halt percentage increase when guardrails fail.
- **Auto-rollback**: revert within minutes based on error budgets.

### Guardrail signals (examples)
- Service SLOs: `5xx rate`, `p95 latency`, `timeouts`, `queue depth`, `CPU`, `OOM`, `db errors`.
- Feature-specific metrics: checkout completion, payment auth rate, cache hit rate.
- Client-side: crash-free sessions, UI error events.

### Rollout controller logic (typical)
- Ramp plan: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% with bake times.
- For each step:
  - Compare canary vs baseline (or pre-change) using metric deltas.
  - If threshold exceeded for N minutes: **freeze** and page on-call.
  - If severe: **auto-rollback** to prior snapshot and set kill-switch.

---

## 6) Governance approvals (segregation of duties + audit)
### Policy-as-code examples
- Prod change to `risk=high` requires:
  - flag owner team approval
  - on-call approver (not the author)
  - security approver
  - linked change ticket
- Any change that targets by sensitive attributes requires privacy review.
- Any “entitlement/billing” flag requires finance approval.

### Auditing
- Immutable audit log: author, approvers, diff, snapshot id, time, reason, ticket link.
- “Who changed prod in last 24h?” queryable.
- Optional tamper-evident storage (append-only log / WORM).

### Access controls
- RBAC by team/service; environment-level permissions.
- Break-glass role: time-bound, MFA, audited, requires incident id.

---

## 7) SDK versioning + compatibility strategy
### Evaluation contract
- Define a stable **Flag Evaluation Spec** (or adopt **OpenFeature** API + your provider).
- Snapshot format has a **schema version**; SDKs declare supported schema versions.

### SDK release process
- Semantic versioning:
  - **PATCH**: bug fixes, perf
  - **MINOR**: backward-compatible features (new operators, attributes)
  - **MAJOR**: breaking evaluation semantics
- Compatibility window:
  - Control plane must emit snapshots compatible with **N-2** SDK major versions (configurable).
- Feature negotiation:
  - Snapshot may include capabilities; SDK ignores unknown fields safely.
- Telemetry includes `sdk_name`, `sdk_version`, `schema_version` to track upgrade progress.

### Deprecation
- Dashboard shows services pinned to old SDKs.
- Automated nudges/tickets when versions reach EOL.
- Block new prod changes requiring features unsupported by deployed SDK versions.

---

## 8) Telemetry/observability (from “change” to “impact”)
### Core telemetry streams
1. **Flag change events** (control plane)
   - Who/what/when; snapshot id; rollout step transitions.
2. **Evaluation telemetry** (data plane)
   - Counts by flag/variation/reason (targeted, default, error).
   - Latency of evaluation, cache freshness, fetch failures.
3. **Exposure events** (analytics/experimentation)
   - User/session id (hashed), variation, timestamp, context attributes (minimized), trace id.
   - Sampling and batching to control cost.

### Operational metrics
- Snapshot distribution lag per region.
- Update fanout success rate; client poll/stream health.
- Cache hit ratio and snapshot size.
- Error budget for “stale config” and “evaluation failures”.

### Correlation
- Attach snapshot id + flag evaluation info to traces/logs (e.g., as baggage fields) for rapid debugging.
- Automated “change impact” view: overlay flag changes with service health charts.

---

## 9) On-call workflows (what happens at 2am)
### SLOs and alerting
- **Flag delivery SLO**: e.g., 99.9% of instances receive new snapshot within 60s.
- **Evaluation SLO**: e.g., 99.99% evaluations succeed locally; p99 eval latency < 1ms.
- Alert tiers:
  - P0: widespread evaluation failures, corrupted snapshots, kill-switch needed
  - P1: distribution lag in a region, streaming outage (clients still on LKG)
  - P2: control plane UI/API down (serving unaffected)

### Standard runbooks
- “Rollback last prod snapshot”
- “Engage kill-switch for feature X”
- “Freeze rollouts globally”
- “Validate snapshot signature/corruption”
- “Region-isolated distribution failure”
- “SDK evaluation bug: force config pin + mitigation”

### Change management integration
- Every prod rollout links to an incident/change record.
- Automated Slack/Teams channel creation per rollout for bake monitoring.
- Optional change freeze windows enforced by policy engine.

---

## 10) Recommended implementation blueprint (pragmatic)
- **GitOps** as source of truth + immutable snapshots.
- **OPA** (or equivalent) for approvals/policy.
- **OpenFeature** SDK API for standardization; custom provider to your data plane.
- **Rollout controller** integrated with monitoring (Datadog/Prometheus) to auto-pause/rollback.
- **Signed snapshots + LKG caching** in SDK/sidecar for resilience.
- **Unified audit + telemetry** with snapshot id correlation everywhere.

If you share your current stack (Kubernetes vs VM, existing CI/CD, observability tooling, regions, and whether you need experiments), I can tailor this into a concrete component list (e.g., exact stores, pub/sub, and rollout controller choice) and an MVP→hardened roadmap.

instruction: Design a microservices observability architecture: standardized telemetry libraries, distributed tracing, metrics cardinality controls, log aggregation, SLO error budgets, alert tuning, and incident review playbooks.
output:
<think>
**Designing the Telemetry Standardization Layer and Reference Data Plane**

I will structure the solution around OpenTelemetry as the single telemetry substrate, since adopting OTLP everywhere eliminates exporter fragmentation and gives me a natural enforcement point for organizational policy. My first architectural decision is a two-tier collector topology: an OTel Agent as a DaemonSet (or sidecar) for low-latency local buffering and first-line processing, and a central HA Gateway where I place the expensive, policy-critical operations — tail sampling, multi-tenant routing, batching. This split matters because agents can't afford tail sampling's full-trace buffering, and I want consistent policy enforcement (scrubbing, filtering) at one chokepoint rather than duplicated per-service. I'll wrap OTel in internal per-language SDKs (`obs-java`, `obs-go`, `obs-node`, `obs-python`) that pin versions, auto-instrument HTTP/gRPC/DB/queue stacks, inject standard resource attributes (`service.name`, `service.version`, `deployment.environment`, `cloud.region`, k8s attributes), and enforce naming conventions. I must ensure the wrapper provides RED/USE helpers, structured logging with trace correlation, and runtime kill switches (disable debug spans, reduce sampling, drop cardinality-heavy labels) so teams can shed telemetry load during incidents. For governance, I'll add CI gates: dependency version policy, metric-name linting, forbidden-label checks, and "telemetry smoke" unit tests that verify baseline signal emission.

**Defining Distributed Tracing, Sampling, and Correlation Invariants**

For tracing, I need to mandate W3C `traceparent`/`tracestate` propagation across HTTP, gRPC, and async messaging — propagating context through Kafka headers and AMQP properties, with explicit linking spans for batch jobs. Sampling is where cost and usefulness trade off, so I'll layer two mechanisms: head sampling in the SDK at a small baseline (1–5%) to cap overhead at the source, then tail sampling at the Gateway to retain 100% of error traces, slow traces above per-route latency thresholds, and traces for specific tenants or canary deploys during rollouts. I must note that head-sampling decisions propagate downstream in OTel, so partial traces stay coherent. Correlation is a first-class design goal: I'll require `trace_id` in every structured log line and enable exemplars on latency histograms so a Grafana panel on a latency spike can pivot directly to representative traces. This gives the one-click alerts → dashboards → traces → logs flow I'm committing to in the design goals.

**Controlling Metrics Cardinality, Histograms, and Log Pipeline Hygiene**

Cardinality is the biggest operational risk for Prometheus-style backends, so I'll define hard, per-metric-family budgets with a three-tier label policy: always allowed (`service`, `env`, `region`, `cluster`), conditionally allowed but bounded (`route`, `method`, `status_code`, `grpc_method`), and forbidden (`user_id`, `account_id`, `email`, `ip`, `request_id`, raw paths, `pod_uid`). The critical edge case is raw URL paths — I'll mandate route-template normalization (`/users/:id` not `/users/123`) via framework hooks. Defense in depth means multiple enforcement layers: `attributes` processor to drop/rename labels, `filter` processor to reject offending metrics, `transform` to bucket dimensions (e.g., collapse `status=200` into `status_class=2xx`), and Prometheus relabeling as last-resort ingestion drop. For latency I'll standardize org-wide histogram buckets (5ms through 10s) and avoid summaries, since summaries can't aggregate across instances; dashboards follow RED for services and USE for infrastructure. For logs, structured JSON only, with a bounded standard field set (`trace_id`, `span_id`, `request_id`, bounded HTTP fields), level policy (ERROR actionable, DEBUG off by default), PII/secret scrubbing and log sampling at the Agent, and tiered retention — hot 7–14 days, warm 30–90, cold archive to object storage for compliance.

**Structuring SLO Error Budgets, Alert Tuning, and Incident Playbooks**

The control plane must tie alerts to customer impact, not infra noise. I'll define per-service SLIs (availability, latency, correctness) with targets like 99.9% availability and p95 < 300ms over 28-day windows (7-day optional for fast feedback), computed via PromQL from the standardized request metrics — good events as non-5xx counts, health-check routes excluded by policy. Error budget policy must change behavior: high burn triggers release freezes, reliability prioritization, and risk review on large rollouts. For alerting, I'll implement a hierarchy (page / ticket / informational only) with multi-window multi-burn rules — page on fast burn (2% of budget in 1h, sustained 5m) and slow burn (5% in 6h, sustained 30m) — because single-threshold alerts either flap or detect slowly. Every alert must carry an impact statement, owner, and deep links to dashboards, trace/log queries, and runbooks; routing groups by service/env/region with maintenance silences, and I'll institutionalize monthly alert reviews plus post-incident threshold adjustments. Finally, the incident playbook standardizes the operational loop: declare/classify SEV, stabilize (rollback, feature flag, load shedding, failover), triage using the correlation pivots I built earlier (burn dashboard → RED by region/route → exemplars → logs by `trace_id`), mitigate with dependency checks, communicate on a cadence, and close with impact window and root cause. The PIR checklist closes the loop by auditing error budget consumption, instrumentation gaps, and alert timing — feeding improvements back into the SDK, label allowlists, and SLO definitions, all stored as code in Git and reviewed like APIs. Concrete defaults: Prometheus/Thanos + Grafana, Tempo/Jaeger, Loki/OpenSearch, Alertmanager → PagerDuty.
</think>

## 1) Design goals & principles
- **Consistency**: every service emits the same baseline signals (metrics, traces, logs) with the same naming + dimensions.
- **Actionability**: alerts tie to **customer impact (SLOs)**, not infrastructure noise.
- **Cost control**: explicit **cardinality budgets**, sampling, retention tiers.
- **Correlation**: one-click pivot between **alerts → dashboards → traces → logs**.
- **Safety**: PII/secret scrubbing at source and in the pipeline; least-privilege access.

---

## 2) Reference observability architecture (data plane)
```text
Microservice (OTel SDK / wrapper lib)
  ├─ Metrics (OTLP) ─┐
  ├─ Traces (OTLP) ──┼──> Node/Sidecar OTel Collector (Agent)
  └─ Logs (OTLP) ────┘        ├─ cardinality guards / scrubbers / sampling
                              └─ forwards OTLP to
                                   Central OTel Collector (Gateway)
                                     ├─ tail sampling, batching, routing
                                     ├─ Metrics -> Prometheus Remote Write -> Cortex/Thanos (+ Grafana)
                                     ├─ Traces  -> Tempo/Jaeger (+ Grafana)
                                     └─ Logs    -> Loki/Elastic/OpenSearch (+ Grafana/Kibana)

Alerting:
  SLO Evaluator (PromQL / Sloth / Nobl9 / Datadog SLOs)
    -> Alertmanager/PagerDuty/Opsgenie
      -> Incident channels + ticketing + status page
```

**Collector placement**
- **Agent (DaemonSet/sidecar)**: low-latency, local buffering, first-line filtering/scrubbing.
- **Gateway (central)**: tail sampling, multi-tenant routing, consistent policy enforcement.

---

## 3) Standardized telemetry libraries (instrumentation plane)
### 3.1 Standard library strategy
- Adopt **OpenTelemetry** as the base (W3C Trace Context propagation).
- Provide an internal **“observability SDK wrapper”** per language (e.g., `obs-java`, `obs-go`, `obs-node`, `obs-python`) that:
  - Pins OTel versions and exporters (OTLP).
  - Auto-instruments common stacks (HTTP/gRPC, DB clients, message queues).
  - Enforces **naming conventions** and **dimension allowlists** (see cardinality).
  - Injects standard resource attributes:
    - `service.name`, `service.version`, `deployment.environment`, `cloud.region`, `k8s.namespace.name`, `k8s.pod.name` (careful), etc.
  - Provides helpers for:
    - RED/USE metrics (server/client)
    - span naming + attributes
    - structured logging with trace correlation

### 3.2 Baseline instrumentation contract (every service)
- **Tracing**: inbound request span + downstream spans; error status set on exceptions; record duration histograms.
- **Metrics** (minimum):
  - `http.server.request.duration` (histogram)
  - `http.server.request.count` (counter)
  - `http.server.active_requests` (gauge) if meaningful
  - dependency client metrics: `http.client.*`, `db.client.*`, `rpc.client.*`
- **Logs**: structured JSON; include `trace_id`, `span_id`, `service.name`, `env`, `request_id` (if available).

### 3.3 Governance & enforcement
- CI checks:
  - dependency version policy (wrapper required)
  - metric name linting + forbidden labels
  - unit tests for “telemetry smoke” (emits baseline metrics/traces)
- Runtime “kill switches” via config:
  - disable debug spans
  - reduce sampling
  - drop high-cardinality labels

---

## 4) Distributed tracing design
### 4.1 Trace context propagation
- Use **W3C `traceparent`/`tracestate`** across HTTP/gRPC and messaging.
- For async workflows:
  - propagate context through message headers (Kafka headers / AMQP props)
  - store correlation IDs for batch jobs with explicit linking spans

### 4.2 Sampling policy (cost + usefulness)
- **Head sampling** at SDK (small baseline, e.g., 1–5%) to cap overhead.
- **Tail sampling** at Gateway Collector (recommended) to keep:
  - 100% of error traces (HTTP 5xx, exceptions)
  - slow traces above latency thresholds per route
  - traces for specific tenants or canary deploys during rollouts
- Ensure sampling decisions propagate downstream (OTel does this when configured).

### 4.3 Trace/log/metric correlation
- Put `trace_id` into logs automatically.
- Enable **exemplars** on latency histograms (Prometheus exemplar support) to jump from a latency spike to representative traces.

---

## 5) Metrics design + cardinality controls
### 5.1 Metric taxonomy
- Prefer **Golden Signals**:
  - **Latency** (histograms; avoid summaries for aggregation across instances)
  - **Traffic** (RPS)
  - **Errors** (error rate)
  - **Saturation** (CPU, memory, queue depth, thread pools)
- Service-level dashboards: RED for request/response services; USE for infrastructure components.

### 5.2 Cardinality budgets (hard rules)
High-cardinality metrics break Prometheus-style systems quickly. Define budgets per metric family and enforce them.

**Allowed labels (example policy)**
- Always allowed: `service`, `env`, `region`, `cluster`
- Conditionally allowed (must be bounded): `route` (templated), `method`, `status_code`, `grpc_method`
- Usually forbidden: `user_id`, `account_id`, `email`, `ip`, `request_id`, raw `path`, `query`, `pod_uid`

**Route normalization**
- Use framework hooks to emit route templates (`/users/:id`) not raw paths (`/users/123`).

**Collector-level protections**
- `attributes` processor to drop/rename offending labels
- `filter` processor to reject metrics with disallowed dimensions
- `transform` to bucket/normalize (e.g., convert `status=200` into `status_class=2xx`)
- Prometheus relabeling to drop labels at ingestion as a last resort

### 5.3 Histograms & buckets
- Standardize latency buckets org-wide (so aggregation works), e.g.:
  - 5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2.5s, 5s, 10s
- Avoid per-endpoint custom buckets unless approved.

---

## 6) Log aggregation architecture
### 6.1 Logging format & levels
- **Structured JSON logs** only (no unstructured printf in production paths).
- Standard fields:
  - `timestamp`, `level`, `service`, `env`, `message`
  - `trace_id`, `span_id`, `request_id`
  - `http.method`, `http.route`, `http.status_code` (bounded)
  - `error.type`, `error.message` (sanitize), `stacktrace` (optional sampling)
- Level policy:
  - `ERROR` for actionable failures
  - `WARN` for unexpected but tolerated conditions (should be rare)
  - `INFO` for lifecycle/audit (rate-limited)
  - `DEBUG` disabled by default in prod; enable temporarily via config

### 6.2 Pipeline & retention
- Prefer OTel logs -> Collector -> log backend (Loki/Elastic/OpenSearch).
- Apply at Agent:
  - **PII/secret scrubbing** (regex + structured key denylist)
  - **log sampling** for noisy lines (keep all errors; sample info)
- Retention tiers:
  - hot searchable: 7–14 days
  - warm: 30–90 days
  - cold archive (optional): object storage for compliance

---

## 7) SLOs + error budgets (control plane)
### 7.1 Service SLO model
Each customer-facing service defines:
- **SLIs** (what you measure): availability, latency, correctness
- **SLO targets** (e.g., 99.9% availability, p95 < 300ms)
- **Windows**: 28d (primary), optionally 7d for faster feedback
- **Error budget**: `1 - SLO` (e.g., 0.1% of requests may fail over 28d)

**Example SLI (availability)**
- Good events: `http_requests_total{status_class!="5xx"}`
- Total events: `http_requests_total`
- Exclude known non-user-impacting routes (health checks) by policy.

### 7.2 Error budget policy (how it changes behavior)
- Define explicit actions when budget burn is high:
  - freeze feature releases for that service
  - prioritize reliability work
  - require risk review for large rollouts
- Track burn during deployments (canary + progressive delivery).

### 7.3 SLO tooling
- Compute SLOs from metrics (Prometheus/Thanos + Sloth, Nobl9, Datadog SLOs, etc.).
- Store SLO definitions as code (Git), reviewed like APIs.

---

## 8) Alert tuning (reduce noise, keep sensitivity)
### 8.1 Alert hierarchy
- **Page** only on imminent/ongoing **SLO burn** or severe availability loss.
- **Ticket** for symptoms that need work but aren’t urgent (e.g., elevated latency but within budget).
- **Informational** (dashboards only) for capacity trends.

### 8.2 Multi-window, multi-burn alerts (recommended)
For each SLO:
- Page when burn rate indicates budget exhaustion soon, e.g.:
  - fast burn: 2% budget in 1h (short window) AND sustained 5m
  - slow burn: 5% budget in 6h AND sustained 30m  
This avoids flapping and catches both sharp outages and slow regressions.

### 8.3 Alert quality controls
- Every alert must include:
  - impact statement (users affected, region, endpoint)
  - links: dashboard, trace query, log query, runbook
  - suggested next steps + owner
- Routing + dedupe:
  - group by service/env/region
  - silence during planned maintenance
- Regular alert reviews:
  - monthly: remove noisy/unused alerts
  - after incidents: adjust thresholds/windows

---

## 9) Incident review playbooks (operational discipline)
### 9.1 Standard incident playbook (runbook template)
1. **Declare + classify**: SEV level based on user impact and scope.
2. **Stabilize**:
   - stop the bleed: rollback, disable feature flag, shed load, failover
3. **Triage with observability pivots**:
   - start from SLO/burn alert dashboard
   - check RED metrics by region/route/status class
   - jump to exemplars/traces for slow/error requests
   - query logs by `trace_id` for failing spans
4. **Mitigate**:
   - dependency checks (db, cache, queue depth, third-party)
   - confirm fix via SLO recovery and error rate normalization
5. **Communications**:
   - internal incident channel updates every N minutes
   - status page updates if user-visible
6. **Close**:
   - note customer impact window, root cause hypothesis, follow-ups

### 9.2 Post-incident review (PIR) checklist
- What was the **SLO impact** (error budget consumed)?
- Timeline: detection → page → mitigate → resolve.
- Contributing factors: deploy, config, dependency, capacity, code path.
- Action items (with owners/dates):
  - instrumentation gaps (missing route label normalization, missing spans)
  - new dashboards/alerts (prefer SLO-based)
  - reliability fixes (timeouts, retries with budgets, circuit breakers)
- Confirm alert tuning:
  - did we page too late/early?
  - noise reduction opportunities

---

## 10) Concrete defaults (starter set)
- **Telemetry standard**: OpenTelemetry (OTLP everywhere)
- **Collectors**: OTel Agent (DaemonSet) + OTel Gateway (HA)
- **Backends** (example stack):
  - Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos/Cortex; visualize in Grafana
  - Traces: Tempo or Jaeger
  - Logs: Loki or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
  - Alerting: Alertmanager → PagerDuty/Opsgenie
- **Cross-linking**: exemplars + trace IDs in logs + Grafana deep links
- **Policies as code**: SLOs, alert rules, sampling rules, label allowlists in Git

---

If you share your environment (Kubernetes vs VMs, cloud, expected service count/RPS, preferred vendors), I can tailor: sampling rates, retention tiers, exact SLO formulas, and a concrete set of dashboards/alerts per service type (HTTP API, async worker, data pipeline).

instruction: Help me roll out a multi-tenant feature flag governance council: charter template, approval workflow, audit logging stack, engineering intake pathways, comms plan, and quarterly KPI review.
output:
<think>
**Designing the Council Charter and Risk-Tiered Decision Rights**

I will structure the solution around a formal Feature Flag Governance Council charter as the anchor artifact, since every downstream workflow, audit rule, and KPI derives its authority from it. The charter must define scope precisely: all runtime-controllable production flags touching tenant isolation, billing/entitlements, privacy/compliance, availability, and customer-visible behavior — while explicitly excluding local dev and compile-time flags so the council isn't drowning in noise. I need to codify three flag archetypes (global, tenant-scoped, emergency kill switch) because the approval workflow and audit schema both branch on these distinctions. For decision rights, I'll embed a RACI matrix that separates policy ownership (Council responsible, VP Eng/CTO accountable) from high-risk approvals (Council Chair accountable) and emergency toggles (Incident Commander empowered, Council informed postmortem) — this prevents the classic failure mode where governance becomes a bottleneck during incidents. Membership must include Support/Customer Success since tenant-facing communication impact is a first-class concern in a multi-tenant model, and the cadence needs three loops: weekly/biweekly approvals, monthly hygiene, quarterly KPI review. I'll also enumerate the council's owned artifacts (policy doc, risk rubric, flag template, audit schema, rollback runbooks) so accountability for each deliverable in the user's request maps to a named owner.

**Structuring the Risk-Tiered Approval Workflow and Intake Pathways**

The approval workflow must be risk-tiered (Tier 0 self-serve through Tier 3 council + security + SRE) because a single approval gate for all flags would either stall engineering or rubber-stamp high-risk changes. I'll design a classification rubric keyed on blast radius: Tier 0 for cosmetic/admin-only, Tier 1 for tenant-scoped functional changes with no auth/data boundary impact, Tier 2 for anything touching entitlements, billing, API behavior, or tenant-visible workflows, and Tier 3 for authN/authZ, tenant isolation, encryption, PII, and cross-region routing. Critically, tier assignment can't rely solely on requester honesty — I'll specify a platform bot that validates proposed tiers against keyword rules (auth/billing/PII/global) and escalates automatically. The seven-stage workflow (intake → automated checks → tier assignment → approvals → rollout → monitoring window → closure) enforces the "fast to turn on, faster to turn off" principle: rollout follows the tenant beta → canary → % → GA progression, monitoring dashboards and exit criteria are mandatory before closure, and expiry dates are enforced with scheduled cleanup. For break-glass, only the on-call Incident Commander may flip kill switches without pre-approval, but an incident ticket with timestamp/actor/reason must auto-open, with council review within 5 business days. Intake pathways mirror the tiers: a self-serve fast path with lint checks, a standard Jira/Linear path with 1–2 day SLA, and a governance form that auto-creates the ticket, change record, and rollout checklist with 5/10-day SLAs for Tiers 2/3. The intake template must capture tenant identifiers/segments, default prod state justification, rollback plan, and comms needs — these fields feed both the audit log and the KPI instrumentation.

**Architecting the Immutable Audit Logging Stack**

For audit logging, I need an event-driven, append-only architecture that satisfies compliance without sacrificing investigability. The flag platform emits audit events (webhook/event bus) into a Kafka/Kinesis/PubSub ingest layer, processed by a stream processor (Flink/Lambda) that validates schema and enriches with directory data. Storage is split by access pattern: an immutable WORM store (S3/GCS with Object Lock) for compliance retention, and a SIEM (Splunk/Elastic/Datadog) for query and alerting. The event schema is non-negotiable and must include event_id, UTC timestamp, actor identity with auth_method, action, flag identity, before/after diffs, tenant_scope, a required reason field linked to a ticket, and correlation_id to join audit events to deploys and runtime telemetry. Multi-tenant privacy drives a key redaction invariant: store tenant IDs, never customer names or emails, and gate full-detail visibility behind RBAC for Security/SRE only. Alerting rules must fire on the highest-risk signals — global flag toggled in prod, bulk tenant-set changes, permission escalations, break-glass usage. Retention follows a 1–2 years searchable plus cold storage pattern, tunable to SOC2/ISO/HIPAA obligations.

**Hardening Comms, KPI Instrumentation, and the 30/60/90 Rollout**

The comms plan must layer audiences and timing: a Week 0–1 launch announcement, Weeks 1–4 enablement (training, office hours, golden-path examples), then ongoing monthly hygiene digests and quarterly leadership reports. Tenant-facing comms are gated by explicit criteria (workflow/billing/deprecation changes) with a message skeleton that always includes rollback assurance. The quarterly KPI review needs a 60–90 minute agenda covering metrics, incidents/near-misses, systemic fixes, policy adjustments, and roadmap — with KPIs grouped into hygiene (owner/expiry coverage >95%, zero expired active flags), delivery speed (median approval time per tier), reliability (MTTD for kill switches, flag-attributable incidents), and multi-tenant correctness (zero cross-tenant exposure events, zero targeting errors). To keep KPIs real rather than manual, I'll wire data sources explicitly: audit logs, ticketing timestamps, incident system, and observability dashboards, producing a one-page scorecard plus an action register. Finally, I'll compress adoption into a 30/60/90 plan — charter ratification and pilot in month one, metadata/TTL enforcement in month two, full council cadence with automated SIEM alerts and live KPI dashboards by day 90 — and close by offering tailoring based on flag platform, compliance regime, and tenant data model, since those three variables determine redaction rules and targeting guardrails.
